w: Brant Point Light has marked Nantucket harbor since 1746, one of America's oldest lighthouse sites. The current tower, listed on the National Register since 1987, is the tenth built here - four predecessors burned or blew down, two were condemned, two just didn't work. Automated since 1965.
s: The tenth lighthouse built on the same spot
_facts: Station established 1746; automated 1965
Current tower is the tenth on the point
Four earlier towers burned or blew down, two condemned, two unsatisfactory
Added to National Register of Historic Places October 28, 1987

w: Built in 1850 above the village of Siasconset, at the island's easternmost point, Sankaty Head Light was among the first US lighthouses fitted with a Fresnel lens, the layered glass that threw its beam out over the Atlantic. Automated in 1965, it still stands sentinel over the bluff today.
s: Siasconset's clifftop light, an early Fresnel beam
_facts: Built 1850, automated 1965
Stands at the island's easternmost point, above Siasconset
One of the first US lighthouses fitted with a Fresnel lens

w: Named for Nantucket-born Maria Mitchell, America's first female astronomer, this observatory founded in 1908 holds over 8,000 glass photographic plates recording the sky from 1913 to 1995. Its Loines site, a kilometer west of town, still houses the historic 7.5-inch Alvan Clark refractor used for stargazing.
s: 8,000 century-old glass plates of the night sky
_facts: Founded 1908, named for astronomer Maria Mitchell
Archive of over 8,000 glass photographic plates, 1913-1995
Loines Observatory houses a historic 7.5-inch Alvan Clark refractor
Association won a 2009 Presidential mentoring award

w: A 46-foot sperm whale skeleton hangs from the ceiling of the Gosnell Hall Whale Hunt Gallery, centerpiece of a museum built around the 1847 Hadwen & Barney Oil and Candle Factory. Its massive lever press once refined whale oil into candles; eleven galleries beyond trace the industry that built the island.
s: A 46-foot whale skeleton over an 1847 candle factory
_facts: Flagship site of the Nantucket Historical Association, restored 2005
Built around the 1847 Hadwen & Barney Oil and Candle Factory
Gosnell Hall holds a suspended 46-foot sperm whale skeleton
Eleven galleries; museum-accredited since 2008

w: At over 30,000 acres, this is the largest conventional National Historic Landmark District by area in the contiguous US - the whole island, plus Tuckernuck and Muskeget. Locally protected since 1955, it expanded federally from just the downtown core and Siasconset in 1975.
s: The largest historic landmark district in the US
_facts: National Historic Landmark District since 1966, expanded 1975 to the whole island
Over 30,000 acres - largest conventional NHL district by area in the contiguous US
Locally designated in 1955, among the earliest US historic districts

w: The original 1784 wooden tower burned in 1816; its stone replacement stood until a March 1984 storm toppled it into the sea. Rebuilt in 1986 as a replica on the thin sand spit where the Atlantic meets Nantucket Sound, it now rests on a five-foot concrete mat built to outlast the currents that took the last one.
s: A lighthouse rebuilt after the sea took it in 1984
_facts: First built 1784; wooden tower burned 1816
1817 stone tower toppled by a storm in March 1984
Rebuilt 1986 as a replica, on the island's northernmost point
Solar-powered, with a 5-foot concrete mat foundation against erosion

w: Dug around 1665 by settlers and Native Americans, Madaket Ditch was Nantucket's first public works project - a mile-long channel cut through marsh to drain meadow and trap fish. Herring, smelt and eels once ran through its weir; a dip net later replaced it. It still runs two to four feet deep at Second Bridge.
s: A 1665 channel dug to catch fish, still tidal today
_facts: First dug circa 1665, Nantucket's first public works project
Connects Long Pond to Madaket Harbor, about a mile long
Historic fish runs included herring, smelt, perch and eels
Still exists at Second Bridge, 2-4 feet deep, tidal
